specAnchors.text: be able to draw the reaction profiles for uncatalysed and catalysed reactions, including the energy level of the intermediate formed with the catalyst

primer.text: Catalysts cheat by geography, not by magic: they open a second route whose energy hill is lower. This note sorts homogeneous from heterogeneous catalysis, draws both the profile humps and the shaded distribution areas, and totals the industrial prizes of speed, cost and atom economy.

modules.title: Catalysis: the lower pathway and its three prizes
modules.opening: A catalyst is not a shortcut magic - it is an alternative route with a lower activation hill. Industry prizes it for speed, for cooler cheaper plants, and for atom economy gains like zeolite-catalysed phenol synthesis.
keyPoints: Catalysis increases reaction rate by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.
Three advantages: more product per unit time, lower energy costs, and potentially better atom economy.
Zeolites in phenol synthesis show how a catalyst can suppress unwanted side products.
The catalyst is unchanged at the end, ready to work again.

low.restatement: The catalysed route crosses a smaller energy hill, so more collisions succeed per second; the same reactants and products emerge, only faster and cheaper.
low.analogy: A mountain pass rerouted through a lower col: the destination is identical, the climb is easier, so more travellers arrive per hour.
low.examPointer: On profiles, draw TWO humps sharing reactant and product levels, the catalysed hump lower, and label both Ea values.

medium.restatement: Lowering Ea enlarges the fraction of collisions that clear the barrier; nothing about collision frequency changes. Industrial wins follow: lower temperature bills, higher throughput, and fewer side reactions trimming waste.
medium.analogy: Lowering a hurdle on a racecourse does not add runners; it just lets more of the same runners clear it.
medium.examPointer: Quote all three advantages when a question says 'state the benefits of industrial catalysis' - speed, cost, atom economy.

modules.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts on the curve
modules.opening: Catalysts come in two phases of life: homogeneous, sharing the reactants' phase, and heterogeneous, standing apart as the industrial standard. On the energy curve, either kind drags the Ea line leftward and the shaded success area balloons.
keyPoints: Homogeneous catalysts share the same physical phase as the reactants, typically all in solution.
Heterogeneous catalysts sit in a different phase from the reactants, most commonly a solid with gaseous reactants.
Heterogeneous catalysis is the most common type in industry.
Lowering Ea means a greater proportion of molecules possess sufficient energy for effective collisions, enlarging the shaded success area.

low.restatement: Same-phase catalysts mingle with reactants molecule by molecule; different-phase catalysts work at their surfaces. Both shrink the energy hurdle, so the beyond-Ea area grows and the rate climbs.
low.analogy: A dance teacher on the floor (homogeneous) versus a climbing wall fixed at the side (heterogeneous) - both help dancers reach the high shelf faster.
low.examPointer: Classify industrial examples correctly: solid iron in ammonia synthesis is heterogeneous; aqueous catalysts with aqueous reactants are homogeneous.

medium.restatement: Phase matching determines the contact mode - bulk collisions versus surface adsorption - but the kinetic effect is identical: reduced Ea, enlarged tail area, faster rate. Industry favours heterogeneous systems for easy separation and reuse.
medium.analogy: A filter that works mid-stream versus one bolted to the pipe wall: different contact, same lowered resistance to flow.
medium.examPointer: On the curve, the catalysed Ea line sits left of the uncatalysed line; the combined light-and-dark shaded areas show the new reactive population.

glossary.definition: A substance providing an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, unchanged at the reaction's end.
A catalyst in the same physical phase as its reactants, such as an aqueous catalyst with aqueous reactants.
A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, typically a solid bed serving a gas stream; the common industrial type.
